In [[mathematics]], the '''Remez inequality''', discovered by the Soviet mathematician [[Evgeny Yakovlevich Remez]] {{harv|Remez|1936}}, gives a [[upper and lower bounds|bound]] on the [[sup norm]]s of certain [[polynomial]]s, the bound being attained by the [[Chebyshev polynomials]].

==The inequality==
Let ''σ'' be an arbitrary fixed positive number. Define the class of polynomials π<sub>''n''</sub>(''σ'') to be those polynomials ''p'' of [[degree of a polynomial|degree]] ''n'' for which

:<math>|p(x)| \le 1</math>

on some set of [[measure (mathematics)|measure]] ≥ 2 contained in the [[closed interval]] [−1,&nbsp;1+''σ'']. Then the '''Remez inequality''' states that

:<math>\sup_{p \in \pi_n(\sigma)} \left\|p\right\|_\infty = \left\|T_n\right\|_\infty</math>

where ''T''<sub>''n''</sub>(''x'') is the [[Chebyshev_polynomials|Chebyshev polynomial]] of degree ''n'', and the [[Uniform norm|supremum norm]] is taken over the interval [−1,&nbsp;1+''σ''].

Observe that ''T''<sub>''n''</sub> is increasing on <math>[1, +\infty]</math>, hence 
:<math> \|T_n\|_\infty = T_n(1+\sigma). </math>

The R.i., combined with an estimate on Chebyshev polynomials, implies the following [[corollary]]: If ''J''&nbsp;⊂&nbsp;'''R''' is a finite interval, and ''E''&nbsp;⊂&nbsp;''J'' is an arbitrary [[measurable set]], then
{{NumBlk|:|<math>\max_{x \in J} |p(x)| \leq \left( \frac{4 \,\, \operatorname{mes}J}{\operatorname{mes}E} \right)^n \sup_{x \in E} |p(x)|</math>|{{EquationRef|⁎}}}}
for any polynomial ''p'' of degree ''n''.

==Extensions: Nazarov–Turán lemma==
[[Inequality (mathematics)|Inequalities]] similar to ({{EquationNote|⁎}}) have been [[mathematical proof|proved]] for different classes of [[function (mathematics)|function]]s, and are known as Remez-type inequalities. One important example is [[Fedor Nazarov|Nazarov]]'s inequality for [[exponential sum]]s {{harv|Nazarov|1993}}:

: '''Nazarov's inequality'''. Let
:: <math>p(x) = \sum_{k=1}^n a_k e^{\lambda_k x} </math>
: be an exponential sum (with arbitrary ''λ''<sub>''k''</sub>&nbsp;∈'''C'''), and let ''J''&nbsp;⊂&nbsp;'''R''' be a finite interval, ''E''&nbsp;⊂&nbsp;''J''—an arbitrary measurable set. Then
:: <math>\max_{x \in J} |p(x)| \leq e^{\max_k |\Re \lambda_k| \, \operatorname{mes}J} \left( \frac{C \,\, \operatorname{mes}J}{\operatorname{mes}E} \right)^{n-1} \sup_{x \in E} |p(x)|~, </math>
: where ''C'' > 0 is a numerical constant.

In the special case when ''λ<sub>k</sub>'' are pure imaginary and integer, and the subset ''E'' is itself an interval, the inequality was proved by [[Pál Turán]] and is known as Turán's lemma.

This inequality also extends to <math>L^p(\mathbb{T}),\ 0\leq p\leq2</math> in the following way

:<math> \|p\|_{L^p(\mathbb{T})} \leq e^{A(n-1) \operatorname{mes}(\mathbb{T} \setminus E)} \|p\|_{L^p(E)} </math>

for some ''A'' > 0 independent of ''p'', ''E'', and ''n''. When

:<math>\operatorname{mes} E <1-\frac{\log n}{n}</math>

a similar inequality holds for ''p'' > 2. For ''p'' = ∞ there is an extension to multidimensional polynomials.

'''Proof:''' Applying Nazarov's lemma to <math>E = E_\lambda = \{x : |p(x)|\leq\lambda\},\ \lambda>0</math> leads to

:<math>\max_{x \in J} |p(x)| \leq e^{\max_k |\Re \lambda_k| \, \operatorname{mes} J} \left( \frac{C \,\, \operatorname{mes} J}{\operatorname{mes} E_\lambda} \right)^{n-1} \sup_{x \in E_\lambda} |p(x)| \leq e^{\max_k |\Re \lambda_k| \, \operatorname{mes} J} \left( \frac{C \,\, \operatorname{mes} J}{\operatorname{mes} E_\lambda} \right)^{n-1} \lambda </math>

thus

:<math>\operatorname{mes} E_\lambda \leq C \,\, \operatorname{mes} J\left(\frac{\lambda e^{\max_k |\Re \lambda_k| \, \operatorname{mes}J}}{\max_{x \in J} |p(x)|} \right)^{\frac{1}{n-1}}</math>

Now fix a set <math>E</math> and choose <math>\lambda</math> such that <math>\operatorname{mes} E_\lambda\leq\tfrac{1}{2}\operatorname{mes}E</math>, that is

:<math>\lambda = \left(\frac{\operatorname{mes} E}{2C \operatorname{mes}J}\right)^{n-1}e^{-\max_k |\Re \lambda_k| \, \operatorname{mes}J}\max_{x \in J} |p(x)|</math>

Note that this implies: 
# <math>\operatorname{mes}E\setminus E_{\lambda}\ge \tfrac{1}{2} \operatorname{mes}E .</math>
# <math>\forall x \in E \setminus E_{\lambda} : |p(x)| > \lambda .</math>

Now

:<math>\begin{align}
\int_{x\in E}|p(x)|^p\,\mbox{d}x &\geq \int_{x\in E \setminus E_\lambda}|p(x)|^p\,\mbox{d}x \\[6pt]
&\geq \lambda^p\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{mes}E \\[6pt]
&= \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{mes}E \left(\frac{\operatorname{mes}E}{2C \operatorname{mes}J}\right)^{p(n-1)}e^{-p\max_k |\Re \lambda_k| \, \operatorname{mes}J}\max_{x \in J} |p(x)|^p \\[6pt]
&\geq \frac{1}{2} \frac{\operatorname{mes}E}{\operatorname{mes}J}\left(\frac{\operatorname{mes} E}{2C \operatorname{mes}J}\right)^{p(n-1)}e^{-p\max_k |\Re \lambda_k| \, \operatorname{mes}J}\int_{x \in J} |p(x)|^p\,\mbox{d}x,
\end{align}</math>

which completes the proof.

==Pólya inequality==

One of the corollaries of the Remez inequality is the '''Pólya inequality''', which was proved by [[George Pólya]]  {{harv|Pólya|1928}}, and states that the [[Lebesgue measure]] of a sub-level set of a polynomial ''p'' of degree ''n'' is bounded in terms of the leading [[coefficient]] LC(''p'') as follows:

:<math>\operatorname{mes} \left\{ x \in \R : \left|P(x)\right| \leq a \right\} \leq 4 \left(\frac{a}{2 \mathrm{LC}(p)}\right)^{1/n}, \quad a>0~.</math>
